questions.question: What two assumptions define an ideal gas, and when does a real gas violate them?
questions.solution: (1) Molecules have negligible volume compared with the container; (2) no intermolecular forces except during instantaneous collisions. A real gas violates these at HIGH pressure (molecular volume matters) and LOW temperature (attractions matter) — which is why real gases liquefy and ideal ones don't. The assumptions are limits, not descriptions.

questions.question: Explain gas pressure microscopically — what exactly pushes the piston?
questions.solution: Countless molecules collide with the piston each second, each transferring momentum 2mv (elastic rebound); the total momentum transfer per unit area per second IS the pressure (P = F/A). Pressure is a statistical average of individual impacts — which is why it is smooth even though each collision is discrete.

questions.question: Why does halving the volume of a gas at constant temperature double its pressure? Give the microscopic reason, not just PV = constant.
questions.solution: At constant T the molecules' average speed is unchanged; halving the volume doubles the NUMBER DENSITY, so each surface is struck twice as often. Twice the collisions per second → twice the momentum transfer per second → double pressure. Constant T keeps each collision's impulse the same; only the collision RATE changes.

questions.question: Why does heating a sealed gas raise its pressure, in terms of molecular kinetic energy?
questions.solution: Absolute temperature is proportional to the average translational KE (½m⟨v²⟩ = 3kT/2). Heating raises molecular speeds, so each collision delivers more impulse AND collisions come more frequently — both raise pressure in a fixed volume. Temperature is a measure of molecular motion, not a separate fluid property.

questions.question: Why is γ (= Cp/Cv) larger for a monatomic gas (5/3) than a diatomic one (7/5)?
questions.solution: Monatomic molecules store energy in 3 translational degrees of freedom only; diatomic molecules also rotate (2 more), so added heat splits among 5 ways instead of 3. More ways to store energy means less goes into translation — temperature rises less, Cv is larger, and γ = 1 + 2/f falls. γ tracks the number of energy-sharing modes.
